audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option studies comparative, European and international law. The second connects law with social change through human rights, criminal justice, sociology and public economics. Maastricht gives more time to compulsory legal doctrine, skills and research.

curriculum.limitation: This comparison follows the standard European Law School bachelor. The third-year electives follow an approved learning plan.

componentNotes.y3-01: Up to 24 EC may be non-law. Introductory electives are capped at 6 EC and a legal internship at 12 EC.
componentNotes.y3-02: Pass the Legal Research challenge before registering. The 12 EC component includes an individual paper, public defence and portfolio.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s European Law School studies national, European and international law from a comparative perspective. The first two years combine compulsory law courses and legal skills. The third year combines restricted electives with an individual legal research project, public defence and portfolio.

notes.text: UCR offers comparative private and constitutional law, criminal law, international law and EU law. Maastricht adds compulsory criminal procedure, more dedicated administrative law and a sequenced legal research and skills curriculum.

Maastricht requires 48 EC of restricted electives and a 12 EC Final Legal Challenge with an individual paper, public defence and portfolio. UCR offers optional independent research alongside its interdisciplinary coursework.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
